questions.title: Object Definition
questions.summary: Non-primitive collections of key-value properties. Variables hold references to objects, allowing shared access and mutation.
questions.answer: An object is a non-primitive JavaScript value that stores properties as key-value pairs. Property keys are strings or Symbols, while values can be any JavaScript type. Variables hold references to objects rather than copying their contents. Multiple variables can reference the same object, and changes through one reference are visible through the others.
questions.underTheHood: Objects have identity and an internal [[Prototype]] link. When accessing a property, JavaScript first checks the object's own properties, then follows the prototype chain if necessary. Objects are compared by identity rather than structural equality.
pitfalls: Objects are compared by identity, not property contents.
const prevents variable reassignment, not object mutation.
Object properties can contain primitives, objects, or functions.
typeof null === 'object' is a historical JavaScript quirk; null is a primitive.
questions.recall: Object → non-primitive → key/value → reference → identity → prototype

questions.title: Object Creation Methods
questions.summary: Create objects with {}, Object.create(), new Object(), constructor F(), class, or factory F(). The main differences involve prototype setup and initialization.
questions.answer: JavaScript provides several object creation patterns. Object literals are the simplest approach. Object.create() creates an object with an explicitly selected prototype. Constructor functions and classes create instances using new, while factory functions return objects directly. new Object() is also available but is generally unnecessary for ordinary object creation.
questions.underTheHood: Object literals normally inherit from Object.prototype. Object.create(proto) assigns proto as the new object's [[Prototype]]. When using new with a constructor, JavaScript creates an object, connects its prototype to the constructor's prototype property, executes the constructor with this bound to the new object, and normally returns that object. Classes use the same prototype-based object model.
pitfalls: Object.create(null) produces an object without Object.prototype in its prototype chain.
Classes use prototype-based inheritance, not a separate inheritance system.
Factory functions do not require new.
Constructor functions called without new may behave differently; class constructors require new.
Object.create() does not invoke a constructor.
questions.recall: {} → literal | Object.create() → explicit prototype | new → constructor | class → instance | Factory F() → returned object

questions.title: Dot vs Bracket Notation
questions.summary: Dot accesses a literal property name; brackets evaluate an expression to obtain a key. Brackets support dynamic keys and names that dot syntax cannot express.
questions.answer: Dot notation accesses a property using a fixed identifier, while bracket notation evaluates an expression to determine the property key. Dot notation is concise for known property names. Bracket notation supports dynamic variables, spaces, special characters, and other property names that cannot be written directly after a dot. Both use the same underlying property lookup mechanism.
questions.underTheHood: JavaScript evaluates the property key and checks the object's own properties. If the property is missing, lookup can continue through [[Prototype]]. Bracket notation converts ordinary keys to property keys, which are strings or Symbols. Optional chaining can prevent an error when accessing properties on null or undefined.
pitfalls: obj.key accesses the literal property named key.
obj[key] evaluates the variable key.
Dot notation cannot directly access property names containing hyphens or spaces.
Optional chaining returns undefined for a nullish base; it does not guarantee that the property exists.
Property lookup may return an inherited property.
questions.recall: Dot → fixed identifier | Bracket → evaluated expression | Both → property lookup

questions.title: Add / Update / Delete
questions.summary: Assignment creates or updates properties; delete removes configurable own properties. Descriptors control whether operations are permitted.
questions.answer: Object properties can be added or updated using assignment. Assigning to a missing key normally creates an own property on an extensible object. Assigning to an existing writable data property updates its value. The delete operator removes a configurable own property. Property descriptors determine whether properties can be written, deleted, or reconfigured.
questions.underTheHood: JavaScript property operations follow internal object methods and property descriptor rules. Writable controls assignment to data properties, while configurable controls deletion and certain descriptor changes. Assigning to an inherited writable data property can create an own property that shadows the inherited value.
pitfalls: const prevents reassignment of the variable, not mutation of the object.
delete cannot remove non-configurable properties.
In strict mode, deleting a non-configurable property throws a TypeError.
delete removes properties, not local variable bindings.
Object.freeze() prevents ordinary property additions, deletions, and value changes on the frozen object, but freezing is shallow.
questions.recall: Add → assignment | Update → assignment | Delete → configurable | Rules → descriptors

questions.title: keys() vs values() vs entries()
questions.summary: keys() returns property names; values() returns values; entries() returns [key, value] pairs. All three return arrays containing own enumerable string-keyed properties.
questions.answer: Object.keys() returns an array of an object's own enumerable string property names. Object.values() returns their corresponding values, and Object.entries() returns [key, value] pairs. These methods exclude inherited properties, non-enumerable properties, and Symbol keys. They are useful for inspecting objects, transforming data, and iterating over properties.
questions.underTheHood: These methods enumerate own enumerable string-keyed properties using JavaScript's defined property ordering rules. Integer-index keys appear first in ascending numeric order, followed by other string keys in insertion order. Symbol keys are excluded. Object.entries() produces nested arrays that can be destructured during iteration.
pitfalls: Inherited properties are excluded from all three methods.
Symbol-keyed properties are excluded.
Non-enumerable properties are excluded.
All three return arrays, not iterators.
for...in also visits inherited enumerable string-keyed properties.
Reflect.ownKeys() includes own string and Symbol keys, including non-enumerable ones.
questions.recall: keys() → keys | values() → values | entries() → pairs | Own + Enumerable + String

questions.title: Reference vs Structural Equality
questions.summary: Objects use identity-based equality. Two objects with identical properties are unequal unless both references point to the same object.
questions.answer: JavaScript compares objects by identity rather than structural equality. Two independently created objects are different even if they contain identical properties. Strict equality returns true when both operands reference the same object. Object.is() also compares object identity. Structural or deep equality requires explicitly comparing relevant properties and nested values.
questions.underTheHood: Objects have distinct identities. Strict equality checks whether two object operands refer to the same object, without recursively comparing properties. Object.is() also compares objects by identity; its differences from === concern certain primitive values, including NaN and signed zero.
pitfalls: Identical object contents do not imply equality.
=== does not perform deep comparison.
Object.is() does not perform structural comparison.
JSON.stringify() is not a reliable general-purpose deep equality solution.
Shallow equality compares top-level values or references; deep equality examines nested structure.
followUps: How would you implement deep equality?
Why does object identity matter in React?
questions.recall: Same ref → true | Different objects → false | === / Object.is() → identity | Deep equality → explicit comparison
